draft.title: Reducing a hazard's impact
card: We cannot stop an earthquake, eruption or landslide. We can cut the harm it does to people and property.
Stronger buildings can stay standing in shaking. Planning rules can keep homes off unstable land, such as steep slopes or flood paths.
Warning systems tell people a hazard is coming. Evacuation plans set out where to go and how to get there, so people can leave in time.
Poorer places often suffer more, as they may have fewer of these measures. The same hazard can then harm more people.
draft.remember: Hazards can't be stopped, but building, planning, warnings and evacuation plans reduce harm.

a.q: A town on a steep hillside bans new homes on its most unstable slopes. How does this reduce the impact of landslides?
opts: Fewer people and homes are in the path of a slide
It warns people that a landslide is about to start
It stops heavy rain from loosening the soil
It makes houses stronger so they survive being hit
a.why: Keeping homes off unstable land means fewer people and buildings are in danger when a slide happens. It does not stop the hazard, and it does not warn anyone or strengthen buildings.
a.clue: Think about who is standing where the slide would go.

b.q: Two coastal towns face the same strong earthquake. Town A has strict building rules and drills. Town B has few rules or plans. Which is the most likely result?
opts: Town B suffers more harm, as it has fewer protections
Town A suffers more harm, as strict rules cost money
Both suffer equal harm, as the earthquake is the same
Town B suffers less harm, as it has fewer buildings
b.why: The same hazard can do different harm. Town B has fewer measures to protect people, so it is likely to suffer more. Equal shaking does not mean equal harm, because preparation changes the outcome.
b.clue: The hazard is the same, so look at what each town did beforehand.

a.best: Fewer people and homes are in the path of a slide

b.best: Town B suffers more harm, as it has fewer protections

problems.detail: "Unstable land, such as steep slopes or flood paths" calls flood paths unstable land. Flood paths are hazardous land but not unstable ground, and floods are not one of the geomorphological hazards in this chapter. Better: "unsafe land, such as unstable slopes".

check.summary: Both questions have one clear right answer, matching the writer's explanations. One small card wording issue: flood paths are given as an example of unstable land, which could mislead students.
